finalResponse:
# Notes Before the Regional Leadership Summit

*Written before the engagement survey pulls, deliberately. Guidance assembled after the survey is not guidance. It's a description of which regions are currently most willing to say encouraging things to HR.*

---

## The word is doing a lot of hiding

"Empowerment" is not a universal good. It's a specific remedy, invented in a specific place, for a specific complaint: that decisions were travelling four levels up and three weeks sideways to get made badly by people with less information. That complaint is real and I share it. But it's *our* complaint — the centre's — and we should be honest that we've named the cure after our own diagnosis and are now shipping it to offices whose illness may be something else entirely.

Some of those offices are not slow because people lack permission. They're slow because nobody has told them what winning looks like, or because the person who has the information is three grades below the person who has the relationship, or because the last person who moved without cover is now managing a small account in a different city and everyone watched.

Those are three different problems. Only one of them is solved by a workshop about ownership.

I'd suggest — and I'd genuinely rather this came from the regional MDs than from me — that we spend the first six weeks not deploying anything, and instead getting one sentence per region: *what is currently escalating that shouldn't, and who benefits from the escalation?* That last clause is the useful one. Every unnecessary approval is load-bearing for somebody.

---

## What's copyable and what isn't

The training programme, the deck, the vocabulary, the town halls, the badge on the intranet — all of this is the easy, visible, measurable layer. It's also the layer that changes nothing on its own, and everyone in every office over the age of thirty knows it, because they've seen this arrive before under a different noun.

What actually constitutes the initiative, and what can't be faked:

Where the signature threshold sits, in currency, in writing. Who can hire without a second conversation. Who can say no to someone senior and remain promotable. What happens, publicly, the first time someone uses the new latitude and gets it wrong. Whether the promotion round in eighteen months rewards the manager whose team decided things without them, or the one who had the tightest grip on their numbers.

That last one is the whole initiative. Everything else is packaging. If the promotion criteria don't move, we're asking people to volunteer for a career disadvantage in exchange for a poster.

So I'd treat the communications programme as necessary and visible — it's how we demonstrate seriousness, and it's what our internal measurement is equipped to detect — and quietly spend the real effort on decision rights, budget thresholds, and the promotion rubric. That ordering is the substance of these notes.

---

## The awkward structural joke at the centre of this

A global initiative mandating autonomy, cascaded from headquarters through a governance committee with regional compliance reporting, teaches the organisation something. Just not the thing on the slide.

People read the medium long before they read the message. If the first experience of "empowerment" is a mandatory module with a completion deadline set by someone they've never met, the lesson learned is: *the centre has a new preference and we should perform it.* And they will perform it, beautifully, and the survey scores will rise, and nothing will happen.

The alternative is less satisfying to manage and much harder to report on: don't announce a culture. Remove approvals, publish the new thresholds, change what gets rewarded, and let the regions notice. Culture is a residue, not an input. It's what's left over after the incentives have finished arguing.

I'd offer this lightly, because it takes the programme away from the programme office, and I'm aware how that sounds coming from me.

---

## Adapting by region — translate the mechanism, not the message

The instinct will be to localise the language. That's the least important adaptation available and the easiest to measure, which is why it will absorb most of the effort if nobody says anything.

The thing worth localising is *how latitude arrives*. The destination can be identical everywhere — the decision gets made by the person closest to it, faster, and holds. How it gets there should look quite different, and I'd resist any attempt to harmonise this into one model.

**Where hierarchy is respected and functional.** Telling a team "you decide now" reads as abdication, or as a test with an unstated right answer. Latitude has to be *conferred*, specifically, publicly, by the senior person, naming the decision and the boundary: *this is yours, up to this amount, and I will carry it if it goes wrong.* Not a philosophy — a delegation, on the record. It looks less like empowerment and more like old-fashioned authority being spent deliberately. It gets to the same place, often faster than the version we prefer, because nobody has to spend three months wondering whether it's a trap.

**Where ambiguity is expensive.** Autonomy without written scope is not freedom, it's exposure. In some offices the gift people want is not a wider open field, it's a bigger box with clearly painted edges. Give the boundaries in writing and be generous inside them. The paradox we should get comfortable with: more documentation can produce more risk-taking, not less.

**Where the group is the unit.** Individual recognition can be a social penalty. Elevating one person's initiative in a team-oriented office may quietly cost that person something we'll never see on a dashboard. Empower the team as the decision-making body; put the recognition on the unit; let them nominate their own voice upward.

**Where relationships carry information.** In offices where the real network is lateral and personal rather than structural, the constraint isn't permission — it's that the org chart doesn't describe who actually knows things. The intervention here is access, not authority: get the people with information into the rooms where decisions happen and most of this solves itself without a programme.

**Where "flexibility" has legal history.** Works councils, co-determination, sectoral agreements, consultation obligations. "Adaptable organisational culture" is a phrase with case law attached in several of our markets. I'd want this drawn once, early, quietly, by someone competent, and treated as an external condition of entry rather than as a topic — because a condition can be designed around, whereas a topic gets reopened in month eight under time pressure by someone with a launch date and a slide they're fond of.

**And the case nobody will raise.** At least one region is probably performing well *because* of tight coordination and clear lines, in a market where speed comes from alignment rather than latitude. Rolling this out there uniformly costs us something real to buy a compliance tick. I'd like the initiative to be able to say, out loud and without it being a career event, that two offices are exempt on merit. If it can't say that, it isn't a strategy. It's a mandate wearing a strategy's clothes.

---

## The layer that will decide this, and it isn't senior leadership

Middle management. We are asking a population whose status, security, and appraisal are constructed almost entirely from control to hand over the control while keeping the accountability, and we are doing it in the same year we're asking them to hold their cost line.

Nobody defects to a system that penalises them. This isn't resistance to change, it's arithmetic, and framing it as a mindset problem — which the programme will want to do, because mindset problems are solvable by training and arithmetic problems are solvable only by giving something up — is how these initiatives die politely.

Three things I'd want in place before a single workshop:

What replaces control as the visible basis of a middle manager's value. If the answer is "coaching," it needs to appear in the appraisal form in a way that beats a good quarter, or it isn't an answer.

Explicit cover for the first three failures, named in advance, at a specific value. Not "we tolerate intelligent failure" — a number, a threshold, and a promise about the appraisal.

Somebody senior visibly declining to reverse a regional decision they disagree with but that wasn't theirs to make. Which brings me to the only intervention in these notes I'd insist on.

---

## What I'd do first

Not a global launch. One deliberately over-reaching pilot in two or three offices chosen for maximum contrast — one where hierarchy is strong and functional, one where it's flat and the constraint is something else entirely — running for a quarter, with a real change in signature thresholds and a real change in one line of the appraisal form. Not a communications pilot. A decision-rights pilot. The comms can follow the evidence rather than substitute for it.

And I'd manufacture one early conflict on purpose. Arrange for a regional team to make a decision that the centre mildly dislikes and clearly has no right to overturn, and then let it stand, visibly, with the centre's fingerprints on the restraint rather than on the reversal.

That single event will teach the organisation more than the entire programme. If it never occurs — if the whole rollout is frictionless and every region reports enthusiastic adoption — we haven't built anything. We've just discovered that people are polite to headquarters, which we knew.

---

## Tests fixed now, before the evidence arrives

Because criteria written afterwards are commentary, and survey questions written afterwards are advocacy.

**Trial is not the gate.** Training completion, town hall attendance, and first-wave survey lift are the equivalent of first purchase — high, easy, and almost meaningless. The gate is whether the behaviour is still there at nine months, after the sponsor's attention has moved.

**One number I'd let into the second meeting:** the count of decisions of consequence made at least one level lower than they were a year ago, and still standing. Everything else is atmosphere.

**Supporting traces, all observable without asking anyone how they feel:** time from problem surfacing to decision; number of approval steps formally deleted, not streamlined; proportion of budget committed without a second signature; how often the centre was informed rather than consulted; and — the one I'd watch hardest — whether anyone who publicly disagreed with a senior leader was promoted afterwards.

**The one-clause test.** Someone in their mid-twenties has to be able to explain the initiative to a peer, in the local language, in one clause, without our slide. If "empowerment," "ownership," "candour," and "psychological safety" have no comfortable equivalent in a given language, that isn't a translation problem to be solved by a better vendor. It's a signal that the concept as framed doesn't exist there, and we should be asking what does.

**At least two regional adaptations should look, to us, slightly wrong.** If every local version resembles the headquarters version, localisation didn't happen; compliance did. The office that implements this in a way that offends our instincts is the one that has actually understood its own market — and that instinct of ours is precisely the local competitive disadvantage we're trying to escape.

---

## A declaration of bias, since it's cheaper to state than to have discovered

I'm predisposed to this initiative. My own preference is for flat, fluid, merit-based teams and authority that has to justify itself by expertise, and I should be assumed to be reading the evidence generously wherever it points that way. Somebody in the room whose instinct runs the other direction should be given a standing licence to say so — not as a courtesy, but because I'll be wrong in a predictable direction and it would be useful to find out early.

---

The failure mode isn't picking the wrong leadership model. It's that by month six the initiative exists as a fact inside our own organisation — with a sponsor, a name, a slot in the plan, ninety-four percent training completion, and not one decision made differently anywhere on earth. At which point the case for continuing has quietly become the case for not having wasted the year.

The defence isn't discipline. It's keeping a genuinely different model alive in parallel the whole way through — a real, resourced, high-clarity, tight-scope alternative running somewhere respectable — so that when the moment comes there's somewhere else to go, and it doesn't have to be invented in a meeting by whoever is most tired.

We aren't installing a culture. We're changing who gets to decide things, and taking something away from people who currently decide them and who mostly don't yet know they're at risk. Every difficulty from here follows from that sentence, and I'd rather it were on the first page than the last.
